item.title: Direct Cultivation of Entangled |CS⟩ Magic States
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Entangled non-Clifford magic states |CS⟩=CS|++⟩ are cultivated directly with no accepted closed-boundary logical-failure mechanisms through fault order two and an operation-count reduction of 34.8% at p=5×10−4 and 37.3% at p=10−3 via optimized d=5→13 surface-code expansion.

Grade 0.480 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Gunsik Min, Jun Heo

Figure

Active locations per accepted |CS⟩ plotted against target binary logical error rate comparing direct |CS⟩ cultivation to a three-T synthesis baseline. Shows direct cultivation requires fewer operations at p=5×10−4 and p=8×10−4, with the cost advantage reversing between 8×10−4 and 9×10−4.

Asks

Can the entangled non-Clifford resource |CS⟩ be cultivated directly with a fault-tolerant branch record, composable code-growth interface, and practical decoder rather than synthesized from independent single-qubit magic states?

Before

Indirect synthesis of |CS⟩ from three logical |T⟩ states via a Clifford+T circuit.

But

Evaluated under a uniform active-location stochastic-Pauli noise model omitting idle memory errors, leakage, coherent errors, and routing. Evaluated for p=10−4 to 10−3; active locations count operations with early-abort accounting rather than spacetime volume.

Tools

commuting Clifford involutions · [6,2,4] classical branch record · verified CAT₇ gadgets · midpoint Steane error detection · four-coset BP+OSD decoder

Abstract

Magic-state cultivation has so far focused mainly on single-qubit non-Clifford resources. We develop a direct cultivation architecture for the entangled state |CS⟩=CS|++⟩. Two commuting Clifford involutions project onto four usable branches related by Pauli-frame updates. A minimal six-bit [6,2,4] record protects the branch label against readout errors that map one valid record to another. Verified CAT₇ gadgets, Steane error detection, CZZ-based controlled checks, and immediate Steane-to-surface expansion form the complete factory. The decoder uses 263 operational detector bits, while 168 additional bits are withheld for later validation. Decoding proceeds through exact low-order resolution, a precomputed higher-order catalogue, and four-coset BP+OSD. Under the stated active-location stochastic-Pauli model, exact enumeration finds no accepted closed-boundary logical-failure mechanism through fault order two, while explicit order-three failure mechanisms exist. Finite-p simulations quantify acceptance, residual syndromes, and decoder workload, and targeted sampling of order-three faults estimates the leading logical-error channels. Optimizing the direct d=5→13 expansion reduces accepted-output operation count by approximately 35--37%. We compare the two routes at the same binary logical-error rate. Direct CS remains cheaper in operation count at the two lower-noise benchmark points even when the three-T route is given pre-existing output patches. The ordering reverses between 8×10⁻⁴ and 9×10⁻⁴. These results show that an entangled non-Clifford state can be cultivated directly with a protected branch record and an explicitly certified fault-order-three output channel.

item.title: Loss-correcting fault-tolerant quantum computing architecture for neutral atoms
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Single-zone transversal-gate layout and loss-aware compilation cut accumulated atom loss per syndrome-extraction round by 1.25× on average (up to 2.15×) and CX routing time by up to 8.5×, reducing logical error rates by up to 212.4× on 100-qubit circuits.

Grade 0.478 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “lattice surgery, logical qubit layout and compilation to a fault-tolerant instr…” · Sanaa Sharma, Yutaka Hirano, Akihisa Goban, Hayata Yamasaki, Shinichi Sunami, Prakash Murali

Figure

CX-routing time in milliseconds (log scale) across benchmark circuits comparing the zoned baseline against the loss-aware layout with 4 AODs. Shorter times reflect higher gate parallelism and fewer trap handoffs.

Asks

How can physical layout, compilation, and decoding be co-designed to mitigate atom loss across fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum computing architectures?

Before

ZAC zoned rearrangement compiler on separate storage/entangling architectures had 2.9× longer average CX routing times (8.4× longer on 32-qubit Ising) and higher logical error rates (e.g. 1.39×10−6 vs 6.56×10−9 on 100-qubit Heisenberg).

But

Circuit-level numerical simulations under rotated surface codes. Relies on continuous mid-circuit atom reloading rates of 2.24×104 to 1.53×107 atoms/s, which exceeds current extraction demonstrations by orders of magnitude.

Tools

Single compute-zone neutral-atom layout · AOD-configuration-aware parallel routing · Transfer-deferred qubit scheduling · Delayed-erasure soft-output surface code decoder · Loss-aware fold-transversal magic state cultivation

Abstract

Neutral-atom arrays are a leading qubit technology for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). A dominant error source on this platform is qubit loss, which accrues with every operation and movement. The presence of loss undermines the promises of existing architectural work. Standard error correction targets stochastic Pauli errors and cannot correct loss, so most FTQC performance analyses are not directly compatible with it. Moreover, compilation and routing decisions, which strongly affect overall loss, are typically optimized against Pauli-error cost models and often remain loss-agnostic, potentially increasing exposure to the loss channel. In this work, we comprehensively model the effect of qubit loss on neutral-atom FTQC and develop a loss-tolerant transversal-gate architecture. We treat loss not as a predetermined error parameter but as a dynamic budget spent across a whole program, allowing us to control it by co-designing layout, compilation, and decoding. We target a physical implementation with no separate storage and entangling zones, eliminating the repeated SLM-AOD handoffs and long-distance shuttling that dominate loss in other layouts. We develop compiler optimizations that maximize gate parallelism while respecting the RF tone budget and AOD bandwidth constraints. Our work couples these with a loss-aware, delayed-erasure decoder and an end-to-end loss-aware magic state cultivation protocol. Overall, we improve accumulated loss per syndrome-extraction round by up to 2.15X against a zoned baseline and reduce logical error rates by over two orders of magnitude versus current architectures. Our framework also informs concrete device targets such as continuous reloading rates, AOD counts, and shuttling trajectory choices. We expect these insights to matter for system architects as neutral-atom hardware scales.

item.title: Accelerating A*-Based Algorithms for Decoding Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Gated belief propagation pre-decoding reduces Tesseract A∗ node expansions by ≈15× at physical error rate p=0.05 (peak reduction 14.79 at pgated=0.1, τ=0.0025) for the [[126,12,d<11]] code, and by 8.8× for the $[[72, 12, 6]]$ bivariate bicycle code, while matching standalone Tesseract logical error rates.

Grade 0.467 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes” · Lamia Yous, Francisco Garcia Herrero, Mark F. Flanagan

Figure

Mean number of A∗ node expansions versus physical error rate p comparing stand-alone Tesseract, ungated BP-Tesseract, and gated BP-Tesseract across T1 and BB codes.

Asks

Can pre-processing syndromes with belief propagation accelerate A∗-based Tesseract search without degrading logical error rates in QLDPC codes?

Before

Stand-alone Tesseract A∗ search decoder and un-gated BP-Tesseract hybrid.

But

Simulated under an i.i.d. symmetric depolarizing noise model, tested only on physical error rates p∈[0.03,0.1] and two specific codes ([[126,12,d<11]] T1 and $[[72, 12, 6]]$ BB).

Tools

Belief propagation · A^* search algorithm (Tesseract) · Oscillation gating mechanism · Sum-product decoding with serial scheduling

Abstract

Quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes represent a promising approach for error correction in quantum computing. The recently proposed Tesseract decoder uses the A* search algorithm that guarantees finding the most likely error pattern. However, practical implementations of Tesseract often involve an extremely large graph, and the inherently sequential nature of the search results in high computational overhead and long runtime. To improve decoding efficiency, we propose a two-stage decoding framework. First, a belief propagation (BP) decoder efficiently processes the syndrome. This step generates hard decisions (a binary error vector) and soft information (per-qubit confidence levels). In non-convergent BP cases, a gating mechanism examines the BP decoder's output to identify and filter out qubits with oscillating confidence values. In these cases, the refined output serves as input to Tesseract, which then attempts to identify and correct any residual errors. This hybrid approach leverages the high speed of BP decoding and delegates the more challenging decoding instances to Tesseract. Numerical results demonstrate a substantial reduction in overall decoding complexity while maintaining the logical error rate (LER) of the stand-alone Tesseract. Across all tested physical error rates, the proposed method achieves at least 5x reduction in the number of expanded nodes in the Tesseract, with a peak reduction of nearly 15x at a physical error rate of p = 0.05 for the [[126, 12, d < 11]] T1 code, and approximately 8.8x at p = 0.05 for the [[72, 12, 6]] bicycle bivariate (BB) code.

item.title: Coded Clifford Measurements for Multiqubit Magic-State Cultivation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Constructing magic-state cultivation records as binary linear codes over Clifford parities saturates the Plotkin bound, resolving distance-four |CS⟩ in 6 logical measurements and |CCZ⟩ in 7 measurements, while reducing active locations in compiled Steane |CS⟩ cultivation by 26.6%.

Grade 0.444 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Gunsik Min, Jun Heo

Figure

Comparison of measurement count, compiled core locations, and active-qubit gate-steps between independent repetition and coded schedules for |CS⟩ and |CCZ⟩ at distance four.

Asks

How to minimize the classical measurement record length and logical redundancy required to cultivate multiqubit non-Clifford resource states without sacrificing fault tolerance?

Before

Independent repetition required 8 logical measurements for distance-four |CS⟩ and 12 logical measurements for distance-four |CCZ⟩.

But

Applies strictly to record-only classical errors; does not eliminate data-coupled fault mechanisms occurring inside measurement gadgets. Validated with 5000 shots per point without full-factory downstream decoder modeling.

Tools

binary linear record codes · third-level Clifford-hierarchy parity checks · Plotkin average-distance bound · exact state-vector Monte Carlo simulation · native-CZZ Steane code compilation

Abstract

Magic-state cultivation suppresses errors by measuring logical Clifford symmetries and discarding inconsistent outcomes. For an entangled resource several branches are accepted, so the retained branch carries a multibit classical record whose corruption produces a logical-frame error. We show that this record layer is exactly a binary linear code. For any third-level Clifford-hierarchy unitary U ∈C₃, the branches UZ(a)|+⟩^(⊗k) are resolved by commuting Hermitian Clifford observables C(v) = UX(v)U^†, so a measurement schedule is a generator matrix and postselection on valid records gives P_wv = O(q^d) at record distance d. A Plotkin bound then limits every binary record, linear or not. The physically realizable Clifford family already saturates it: at distance four, six logical measurements suffice for |CS⟩ and seven for |CCZ⟩, against eight and twelve for independent repetition. Restricting to fault-tolerantly measurable parities therefore costs nothing in record length. The saving survives compilation: in a native-CZZ-assisted Steane realization the [6,2,4] CS schedule is the unique minimum-cost distance-four solution, reducing the cultivation core by 26.6% in active locations, and exact state-vector simulation without a final ideal code-space projection confirms higher acceptance and roughly half the residual Steane-boundary weight. Coding thus reduces logical redundancy and compiled overhead together.

item.title: Noise Limits on Fault-Tolerant Fermionic Quantum Computing
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Depth-independent upper bound on local depolarizing noise for fermionic quantum computation is p=(8−26)/5≈62% (0.6202). Above this depolarizing rate, all 2-qubit parity-preserving non-Gaussian gates map into convex Gaussian channels.

Grade 0.432 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Owen Allison, Luke Coffman

Figure

Concurrence parameters Δ+ and Δ− versus depolarizing probability p for SWAP, alongside state commutator with parity [hoU,p,P]. Shows Δ+ crossing zero at p≈0.62.

Asks

What is the upper bound on local depolarizing noise after which fault-tolerant fermionic quantum computing with matchgates and non-Gaussian gates becomes impossible?

Before

Local depolarizing noise limit was ≈45% for Clifford + T circuits (Bravyi, Browne, Calpin, Campbell, Gosset, Howard 2016).

But

Restricted to 2-qubit parity-preserving gates followed by local depolarizing noise, assuming noise-free matchgates and Gaussian input states.

Tools

Matchgate with non-Gaussian resource gate set · Uhlmann-Wootters concurrences for 4-mode fermionic states · Fermionic Choi state representation · Local depolarizing noise model

Abstract

Determining the highest amount of noise that quantum circuits can handle is an interesting and crucial task in the development of fault-tolerant quantum computation. Previous work has constrained this upper limit for local depolarizing noise to ≈45~% for circuits constructed using the universal Clifford with T gate set by finding the noise threshold where the gate set loses universality. In this work, we use a similar method with the matchgate with non-Gaussian resource universal gate set to find a limit of p=(8 - 2 √6)/5 or ≈62~% for fermionic quantum computing that is independent of circuit depth. To do this, we use Uhlmann-Wootters concurrences for a 4-mode fermionic Choi state representing a resourceful gate combined with local depolarizing noise to determine when the combined channel is convex Gaussian. These bounds are not directly comparable due to differences in noise model making the bound of ≈62~% the best known for fermions.

item.arxave:tools: Matchgate with non-Gaussian resource gate set · Uhlmann-Wootters concurrences for 4-mode fermionic states · Fermionic Choi state representation · Local depolarizing noise model
item.arxave:abstract: Determining the highest amount of noise that quantum circuits can handle is an interesting and crucial task in the development of fault-tolerant quantum computation. Previous work has constrained this upper limit for local depolarizing noise to ≈45~% for circuits constructed using the universal Clifford with T gate set by finding the noise threshold where the gate set loses universality. In this work, we use a similar method with the matchgate with non-Gaussian resource universal gate set to find a limit of p=(8 - 2 √6)/5 or ≈62~% for fermionic quantum computing that is independent of circuit depth. To do this, we use Uhlmann-Wootters concurrences for a 4-mode fermionic Choi state representing a resourceful gate combined with local depolarizing noise to determine when the combined channel is convex Gaussian. These bounds are not directly comparable due to differences in noise model making the bound of ≈62~% the best known for fermions.
